Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
• 2-day history of constant, gradually worsening suprapubic/below-umbilical burning pain with urinary frequency and pink-tinged urine in an otherwise healthy reproductive-age woman; most consistent with uncomplicated acute cystitis treated empirically with trimethoprim.

History:
• Presenting complaint & timeline  
  – Burning pain just below umbilicus × 2 days; gradual onset, now worsening but still able to ambulate.  
  – Associated: ↑ urinary frequency, pink urine, mild nausea, subjective fever/diaphoresis.  
  – No dysuria, no flank pain, no vomiting, bowels currently normal (constipation last week resolved), no diarrhea.  
  – Review of systems: No cardiorespiratory, neurologic, or visual symptoms.

• Past medical/surgical: Generally healthy; no prior surgeries; no similar episodes reported.  
• Allergies: Not discussed.  
• Medications: Etonogestrel (Implanon) inserted 1 yr ago; no other regular meds.  
• Gynecologic/sexual: Sexually active with single partner; last intercourse 4 days ago. LMP ~2 weeks ago. Implanon only contraception; prior STI screen negative 6 months ago.  
• Social / preventive: Accountant; lives with 2 roommates. Non-smoker; social alcohol use.

Examination:
• Telephone consult – no physical examination or vitals available.

Impression:
1. Acute uncomplicated cystitis ‑ high likelihood. Supporting: suprapubic pain, urinary frequency, pink urine (possible hematuria), mild systemic features without flank pain.  
2. Early appendicitis – considered (peri-umbilical pain, nausea, low-grade fever) but less likely given urinary features and lack of RLQ localization.  
3. Pregnancy-related cause (incl. ectopic) – unlikely with Implanon and recent normal period but not excluded; pregnancy test advised.

Plan:
• Empiric antibiotics: Trimethoprim 300 mg (standard tablet) 1 tab PO BID × 3 days (e-script sent to patient’s pharmacy).  
• Symptomatic care: Acetaminophen for pain; maintain hydration; may try cranberry juice.  
• Diagnostics: Home urine pregnancy test today/tomorrow; consider urinalysis & culture, CBC, and abdominal exam if no improvement or worsening.  
• Safety-net advice: Return/seek care if worsening abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, urinary symptoms, visible hematuria, or no improvement in 48–72 h.  
• Follow-up: Telephone or in-person review in 3–5 days or sooner if concerns.

Quality checks:

● Missing but expected: Patient’s age, weight, drug allergies, exact antibiotic dose strength confirmed, baseline vitals, physical abdominal exam, urinalysis, pregnancy test result, formal follow-up appointment date.  
● Conflicts: Transcript notes no dysuria whereas cystitis typically includes dysuria (acknowledged in DDx). Name alternates between “Tim” and “Kim” (likely transcription error).  
● Transcript quality: Telephone consult; no examination data; several verbal pauses; minor name inconsistency; otherwise clear history.
